chapter_theme: Tapas (தவம்): those who withdraw and let go of attachment are beyond fear, death and the turn of day and night; only those with the Lord's grace know what tapas is; it ends birth where asking only wins wealth; no threat shakes the true ascetic, and the Lord comes near only to such. Yet the chapter ends by saying tapas is needed only until the samadhi of knowledge is reached.
structure_note: Praise of tapas and the tapasvin (1624 to 1630), then the inward look that replaces learned talk (1631), and a closing verse (1632) that limits tapas to a stage, leading into the next chapter.

1624.reading: For those excellent ones who have withdrawn and become steady and let go of attachment, the heart does not tremble, Yama is not there, nor suffering, nor night and day, nor any fruit of deeds to undergo.
1624.nuance: ஒடுங்கி is withdrawal, of the senses into the mind or the mind into stillness. The list of absences is built so that letting go of பற்று, named only in the last word, is the cause of all of them. இராப்பகல் இல்லை may also be a yogic reference to a state beyond the sun and moon breaths.

1625.reading: None but those who have received the Lord's holy grace know the nature of this great tapas, or all the precious lives and the appearing of the wide earth, or the greatness of what true tapas does.
1625.nuance: The verse makes grace prior to tapas: even knowing what tapas is depends on it. The first line, all lives and the appearing of the world, can be read as more things grace reveals or as the effects of tapas itself; the grammar allows both.

1626.reading: People who ask for many things, not knowing what birth is, get the wealth they wanted with honour; those who do great tapas without forgetting win the greatness of ending birth.
1626.nuance: பிச்சைசெய் மாந்தர் may be beggars in the plain sense or worshippers who beg favours of the Lord; the contrast is between asking for goods and the tapas that seeks no goods but an end to birth. The verse grants that asking works; it ranks it lower.

1627.reading: Whoever comes to unsettle the great ones who sit enduring hardship in their fair tapas, even Indra himself, their minds are set right upon Siva.
1627.nuance: Indra sending distractions to break an ascetic's tapas is a familiar puranic motif; the verse answers it by placing the ascetic's steadiness in Siva rather than in his own strength.

1628.reading: Hidden, yet not hidden, he does not appear to the eye: he of the spreading matted hair and the colour of fresh gold, wearing the white moon, cannot be approached except by those of rare tapas, and is to be worshipped without delay.
1628.nuance: கரந்தும் கரந்திலன், hiding yet not hidden, is a paradox common in Saiva hymns: present everywhere but not seen. The verse gives a full iconographic image while denying that the eye sees it.

1629.reading: The First, our Lord, who set the blissful birth to be reached later and set what must come first, reveals himself when the time to reach him comes; it is the mind, set to reach him firmly, that does this.
1629.nuance: இன்பப் பிறப்பு, a birth of joy, may be a heavenly birth or the birth in which release comes; what is 'set to come first' (முன்னெய்த வைத்த) is not named, and in this chapter may be tapas. The last line's மன் எய்த may be 'to reach firmly' or 'to reach the king'. The chain of 'set' (வைத்த) makes the Lord the arranger of the soul's sequence.

1630.reading: Caught in the midst of the uproar when ministers, troops of elephants and kings rise in enmity, those who kept their gaze on the knowledge they had set up and on the trustworthy one, and stayed unblinking and unharmed, are the people of tapas.
1630.nuance: ஆத்தம் is āpta, the trustworthy one or the trustworthy word, traditionally the Lord or the scripture he gives. The scene is literal war, and the claim is that the tapasvin's stillness holds even there. இமைத்தழியாது can be 'without blinking' or 'without perishing in a blink'.

1631.reading: Leave the cleverness of reciting the shastras and, for the space of a moment, turn back and look within; that look, fixed like a nail driven into green wood, drives off the births that bind.
1631.nuance: மாத்திரைப் போது is the length of a single measure, the shortest unit of time. பசுமரத்து ஆணி, a nail in green wood, is the proverbial image of what goes in easily and holds firm. The verse sets a moment's inward look against a lifetime of scriptural talk.

1632.reading: Tapas is needed if one is to reach knowledge, but not needed once the samadhi of knowledge is in hand; tapas is not needed by those on the path of the companion, and they do not know the word that says 'no tapas'.
1632.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are clear: tapas is a means that falls away. Line 3 (மச்ச கசமார்க்கத்தோர்க்கு) is probably corrupt; if it is சகமார்க்கம், it is the 'path of the companion', traditionally the yoga stage of the Saiva fourfold path. Line 4 is obscure: it may mean they don't need tapas because they are past the debate, or that they never learned the teaching that tapas is unneeded.

links.note: Both put the ascetic beyond death: the Kural says those who gain the power of tapas can leap past Death, Tirumular that for those who have withdrawn and let go, Yama is simply not there.
The Kural commends tapas because whatever one wants is gained as one wants it. Tirumular separates getting what one wants, which mere asking achieves, from tapas, whose greatness is ending birth.
Both define the ascetic by firmness under pressure: the Naladiyar's blessed push aside troubles that would break their vows, Tirumular's stay unblinking amid kings at war.

Both set inner work against learned talk: the Naladiyar calls those who prattle of grammar and astrology the greatest fools, Tirumular tells the reader to leave clever shastra-recitation for a moment's inward look.

Kural 25 makes Indra, lord of the wide heavens, witness to the strength of one who has quenched the five (ஐந்தவித்தான் ஆற்றல் ... இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி); in 1627 Indra himself (இருந்திந்திரனே) comes to unsettle those who sit in tapas, and their minds stay set on Siva. In both Indra is the measure of the ascetic's power; 1627 places the ascetic's firmness in Siva rather than in his own strength.

1625 says none but those with the Lord's grace know what tapas is (திருவருள் பெற்றவர்க்கல்லாது); 1628 says the Lord cannot be approached except by those of rare tapas (அருந்தவர்க்கல்லால் அணுகலுமாகான்). Together they make a circle the chapter does not resolve: grace is needed to know tapas, and tapas is needed to approach the giver of grace.

source_issues: 1632 line 3 reads மச்ச கசமார்க்கத்தோர்க்கு, probably corrupt; perhaps for (அ)ச்ச சகமார்க்கத்தோர்க்கு.
